stem: A $2.0\text{ kg}$ trolley moving at $3.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ collides with a stationary $1.0\text{ kg}$ trolley and they move off together. What is the speed of the trolleys after the collision?
markscheme: Momentum is conserved: $2.0 \times 3.0 = 3.0\,v$, so $v = 2.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

stem: A resultant force of $12\text{ N}$ acts on a $4.0\text{ kg}$ object for $2.0\text{ s}$. What is the change in momentum of the object?
markscheme: Impulse $= F\Delta t = 12 \times 2.0 = 24\text{ N s}$ = change in momentum. The mass is not needed.

stem: A car of mass $1200\text{ kg}$ travelling at $15\text{ m s}^{-1}$ brakes uniformly and comes to rest in $3.0\text{ s}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the deceleration of the car.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average braking force on the car.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State Newton's third law of motion. Identify the force that pairs with the frictional force of the road on the car.
markscheme: If body A exerts a force on body B, then B exerts a force of equal magnitude and opposite direction on A (forces of the same type)
The frictional force of the car (tyres) on the road, acting forwards

parts.label: d
parts.text: A seat belt stretches slightly during a sudden stop. Outline why this reduces the force on a passenger.
markscheme: The change in momentum of the passenger is the same
but it takes place over a longer time, so $F = \Delta p / \Delta t$ is smaller

stem:
A student pulls a trolley along a horizontal bench with different constant forces $F$ and measures the acceleration $a$ each time.

F / N: 0.50, 1.00, 1.50, 2.00
a / m s⁻²: 0.24, 0.51, 0.74, 1.01

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to determine the mass of the trolley.
markscheme: Mass is the gradient of a graph of $F$ against $a$ (or uses $\Delta F / \Delta a$ from two well-separated points)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a graph of $F$ against $a$ might not pass exactly through the origin.
markscheme: Friction acts on the trolley, so some of the applied force is needed before it accelerates (or any reasonable systematic error, e.g. a zero error in the force meter)
